sources.title: Rowe et al. (2016): seven-year randomized LNG-IUD vs TCu380A study
sources.design: Open-label randomized multicenter trial, 3,755 analyzed; primarily parous women, 20 centers, nine countries
sources.finding: Cumulative 7-year pregnancies per 100: LNG 0.5 (SE 0.2), copper 2.5 (SE 0.4); discontinuation 70.6 vs 40.8. Copper removals for heavier bleeding; LNG removals for reduced bleeding or amenorrhea.

sources.coi: Authors declare none; manufacturer/device relationships and acknowledgments not independently corroborated.

sections.title: Compare birth control methods
sections.summary: Compare hormone exposure, pregnancy prevention, convenience and future fertility without a universal best-method score.
sections.keywords: contraception birth control compare effectiveness hormone free low hormone best method failure rate
paragraphs: The chart uses estimated pregnancies per 100 users during the first year of ordinary use. The figures are population summaries, not a personal prediction. Methods that do not require remembering a daily or per-sex action generally have less opportunity for user error.

Zero added contraceptive hormones: copper IUD, barriers and trained fertility awareness. No estrogen: hormonal IUD, implant, progestin-only pill and injection. Lower circulating progestin: LNG IUDs compared with the selected systemic formulations studied. No estrogen does not mean no hormones.

Consider menstrual bleeding, pain, STI protection, pregnancy plans, ability to stop or remove the method, health conditions and cost/access. A clinician can help assess whether a method is medically suitable; the decision belongs to the person using it.
Compare by outcome, not a single health score

A lower contraceptive failure rate is not a measure of mental health or long-term harm. The decision guide separates hormone exposure, pregnancy prevention, insertion burden, bleeding, and time to fertility. Eligibility and individual preferences can change which options are reasonable.

sections.title: Copper IUD: no added hormones
sections.summary: A long-acting reversible, hormone-free device. Bleeding and cramps are the principal trade-offs to explore.
sections.keywords: paragard copper coil non hormonal iud copper toxicity cramps heavy periods
paragraphs: A copper-bearing device in the uterus interferes with sperm function and fertilization, without delivering estrogen or progestin. Ovulation is not deliberately suppressed. A qualified clinician inserts and removes it.

The WHO-led randomized study observed low cumulative pregnancy rates with both types of IUD. Copper users more often requested removal because of heavier bleeding, while LNG users more often requested removal because of reduced or absent bleeding. These findings depend on the products and populations studied.

Discuss existing heavy periods, anemia, pelvic infection risk, anatomy, copper allergy or Wilson disease if relevant, and pain-management options. Expulsion and perforation are uncommon but important; individual risk varies with insertion timing. No self-insertion or removal.

The evidence does not support routinely delaying attempts simply to clear contraceptive hormones after copper IUD removal. Removal must be arranged with a clinician. Seek advice if pregnancy is suspected with an IUD in place, especially with pain or bleeding.

Human copper measurements have been inconsistent and largely assessed total rather than free copper. This does not establish systemic poisoning from routine use, or rule out all effects. Sexual-function studies are mixed; pain and heavier bleeding can influence sexual wellbeing even without added hormones.

The same uterine placement discussion applies to both copper and hormonal IUDs. A 2026 survey did not identify a significant difference in recalled pain, but cannot demonstrate equal pain. Ask about anesthetic options and a plan to pause if needed.

sections.title: Hormonal IUDs: local release, not zero exposure
sections.summary: Levonorgestrel is released mainly within the uterus; some reaches the bloodstream. Compare bleeding effects, device dose and duration.
sections.keywords: mirena kyleena skyla liletta levonorgestrel hormonal coil local low dose iud progestin
paragraphs: Levonorgestrel thickens cervical mucus and alters the uterine lining. Ovulation can continue. Different devices have different hormone loads and approved durations; a smaller reservoir is not a proven overall safety advantage.

A Bayer-affiliated pharmacokinetic analysis found lower circulating LNG for the IUDs studied than for its selected pills and implant. This is a drug-concentration comparison, not evidence that symptoms or long-term health outcomes are proportionally reduced.

Spotting can occur early, followed by lighter or absent bleeding. Some people value this; others prefer regular bleeding. The seven-year trial also recorded removals for symptoms compatible with hormonal effects.

Insertion and removal require a clinician. Discuss current/past breast cancer, bleeding concerns, pelvic conditions, procedural pain and desired fertility timing. Seek prompt care for possible pregnancy with an IUD.
Long-term outcomes are not all explained by blood hormone levels

Observational VTE data are reassuring for LNG IUDs in one Danish cohort, but breast cancer findings vary by formulation. A 2026 registry study also reported a meningioma association with high-dose LNG IUD; earlier French data on surgical meningioma differ. These are rare-event observational findings, not a causal ranking or proof that a lower-dose device is safe.

sections.title: Combined pill, patch & vaginal ring
sections.summary: Estrogen plus progestin delivered systemically. Compare convenience, cycle benefits and eligibility.
sections.keywords: combined pill oral contraceptive birth control pills estrogen ethinyl estradiol patch nuvaring ring
paragraphs: All three combined methods use estrogen and progestin; administration differs. A ring or skin patch is not automatically a low systemic hormone method. Routine use schedules and interactions vary by product.

Combined methods can offer predictable bleeding and help some cycle-related symptoms. The presence of estrogen matters for vascular risk; evaluate migraine with aura, clot history, high blood pressure, smoking at older ages and early postpartum status with a clinician.

Trial reviews do not establish a large average weight effect for combined pills or patches. Cancer associations differ by cancer type: observational evidence links oral contraceptives to increased risks for some cancers and reduced risks for others. Neither finding determines a single person's balance.
Fertility may return after stopping; a temporary delay in conception does not imply permanent infertility. Review the timing of stopping and alternative protection until ready.
Beyond the pill: arterial and venous events

Registry research associates combined pills, patch and ring with increased clot risk. Arterial stroke and myocardial infarction are distinct outcomes. Choice of estrogen and progestin matters, but a lower estimate for a formulation cannot override clinical eligibility.

sections.title: Progestin-only pill (mini-pill)
sections.summary: No estrogen, but a systemic progestin. A daily method with formulation-specific timing rules.
sections.keywords: mini pill minipill pop norethindrone norgestrel drospirenone estrogen free pill opill
paragraphs: This pill contains a progestin and no estrogen. Formulations differ in how consistently they suppress ovulation and their missed-pill instructions. The absence of estrogen does not eliminate all side effects.

Daily adherence and interactions matter. Unscheduled bleeding may occur. Review relevant conditions, especially breast cancer history and medication interactions, and use product-specific guidance rather than a generic missed-pill rule.
The weight and breast cancer literature does not justify assuming every progestin-only formulation has the same effect. The available studies differ in design, populations and endpoints.

The 2025 cohorts observed progestin-only pill associations with VTE, arterial stroke and breast cancer; relative and absolute risks depend on population, product and time window. Do not assume no estrogen means no vascular or cancer concerns.

sections.title: Arm implant & contraceptive injection
sections.summary: Estrogen-free systemic methods. The implant is removable; the injection has a longer tail after stopping.
sections.keywords: nexplanon etonogestrel implant depo provera dmpa shot injection arm birth control
paragraphs: The arm implant releases progestin continuously and is placed/removed professionally. The depot injection releases medicine over time and cannot be removed once given. Product-specific approved duration needs current label verification.

Unpredictable bleeding may occur. Some DMPA studies report greater weight gain than comparison groups; evidence across progestin methods is limited. DMPA's bone-density considerations are a separate clinical discussion, not a reason to assume all progestins have identical effects.

The prospective preconception cohort found the longest temporary conception delay after injectable contraception. That association does not imply permanent infertility or establish a mandatory washout. Discuss the timing of the last injection if pregnancy is planned.

DMPA is associated with bone density loss, with recovery documented after discontinuation; actual later fracture risk is harder to establish. French and Danish registry studies found meningioma associations for injectable medroxyprogesterone. Implant findings cannot be borrowed from DMPA, or vice versa.
Mood evidence that challenges a simple hormone ranking

In a single-site ECHO ancillary randomized study, the injectable group had fewer moderate/severe depressive symptoms than the copper IUD group at 12 months. The study lacked baseline mood data and had a strong local method preference. It neither proves injections improve mental health nor shows hormone-free methods cause depression.

sections.title: Condoms, diaphragm, cap & nonhormonal gels
sections.summary: Hormone-free options used around sex. Correct and consistent use matters; condoms also reduce STI risk.
sections.keywords: condom condoms barrier diaphragm cervical cap spermicide sponge phexxi vaginal ph gel nonhormonal
paragraphs: External and internal condoms, diaphragms, cervical caps and sponges work by impeding sperm. Some products use spermicide or a vaginal pH modifier; their instructions and irritation risks differ.

Appropriate condoms reduce transmission of HIV and other STIs but not all infections or exposures. Most other contraception does not provide this protection. Natural-membrane condoms are not reliable for STI prevention.

No contraceptive hormone exposure or pharmacologic delay after stopping. The burden of using them correctly every time matters for pregnancy prevention; fitting, supply, comfort and partner cooperation vary.

sections.title: Fertility awareness & cycle tracking
sections.summary: Hormone-free methods based on fertility signs, not simply guessing the next period.
sections.keywords: natural family planning nfp symptothermal temperature mucus ovulation cycle tracking app calendar withdrawal rhythm natural cycles
paragraphs: Different approaches use calendar rules, cervical mucus, basal temperature or urinary hormone information. They have distinct evidence and training requirements. Avoiding unprotected intercourse during identified fertile days is central.

The systematic review found 53 eligible studies, none rated high quality by its authors. Estimates differed substantially across approaches and studies; a generic period tracker cannot inherit the effectiveness of a validated method.

Cycle variability, postpartum changes, recent hormonal contraception and inconsistent observations can complicate interpretation. Withdrawal is a separate behavioral method; evidence on trained fertility awareness does not establish its reliability. Do not use Everwell's pregnancy calendar as contraception or a fertility predictor.

sections.title: Hormones, mood, weight & long-term risks
sections.summary: Explore conflicting evidence on symptoms and serious outcomes separately, without equating lower drug levels with guaranteed safety.
sections.keywords: birth control hormones estrogen progesterone progestin depression mood anxiety libido weight cancer blood clots thrombosis side effects
paragraphs: Randomized trial synthesis found no average worsening of depressive symptoms among studied adults; a Danish registry study observed associations with depression-related outcomes, particularly in younger users. Different endpoints, selected trial participants and nonrandom exposure explain why results need not agree. Individual symptoms deserve attention.

Combination-method trials do not show a large average causal weight effect; progestin-only evidence is limited, with signals for DMPA. Body changes are not inevitable and method-specific estimates cannot be generalized.

A contemporary Danish registry study identified differences in venous clot associations between products. Combined hormonal methods require attention to estrogen-related eligibility. A nonsignificant result for IUDs is not proof of zero risk.

Recent hormonal prescriptions were associated with breast cancer in a UK observational analysis; oral contraceptives also have associations with reduced ovarian and endometrial cancer risk. Absolute risk varies with age and history. Review current or previous breast cancer with a clinician.

New severe mood symptoms warrant professional support. Chest pain, sudden breathing trouble or one-sided leg swelling/pain can be serious and need urgent assessment. Do not stop or change contraception without considering pregnancy prevention if still desired.

sections.title: Stopping birth control & trying for a baby
sections.summary: Compare temporary delays in conception, what is known about lasting fertility, and preconception planning.
sections.keywords: return fertility after birth control stop pill iud removal detox washout infertility conceive trying pregnancy ovulation planning
paragraphs: A prospective cohort followed 17,954 people planning pregnancy. Some prior hormonal methods were associated with temporary conception delays; injectable contraception showed the longest delay. Fecundability means the chance of pregnancy per cycle, not proof that ovulation was absent.

A separate review pooled 12-month pregnancy outcomes after stopping reversible contraception. The estimate was 83.1% (95% CI 78.2–88%), across heterogeneous observational studies. It cannot predict an individual's chance or prove every method is equivalent.

These studies do not establish a required hormone-clearing period before trying. Fertility can return before a first recognizable period. For IUD or implant removal, plan a clinician visit; for injections, discuss potentially longer timing. Maintain protection until pregnancy is wanted.

Review medications, existing conditions, vaccinations and preconception nutrition with a clinician before trying. If cycles do not return or conception is delayed, ask for assessment rather than assuming contraception caused infertility.

A prospective cohort found little association between miscarriage and prior use of pills, IUDs, ring or implant; patch and injection results were uncertain. Danish live-birth data did not show increased major birth defects after recent pill use. These studies are not guarantees about individual pregnancy outcomes.

Multinational survey evidence broadly supports the longer temporary delay with injectable contraception, while exact timing differs from the North American/Danish prospective cohort. Age, underlying fertility and method choice matter.

sections.title: Emergency contraception, postpartum & permanent options
sections.summary: Special situations require separate evidence and eligibility; emergency methods are not routine contraception.
sections.keywords: plan b ella morning after emergency contraception breastfeeding lactational amenorrhea postpartum vasectomy tubal ligation permanent sterilization
paragraphs: Copper IUD and emergency contraceptive pills are time-sensitive options in CDC guidance. Contact a clinician or pharmacist promptly after unprotected sex or method failure; different pills and subsequent hormonal methods can interact. A trial also studied the 52-mg LNG IUD for emergency use, but this is not evidence for every hormonal IUD or a self-directed protocol.

Postpartum and breastfeeding timing affect method eligibility. Lactational amenorrhea is temporary and requires all three conditions: no return of menstruation, full or nearly full breastfeeding, and less than six months since delivery. If any condition changes, it no longer meets the definition.

Vasectomy and tubal procedures are intended to be permanent, so they are different from reversible planning. Vasectomy is not immediately effective; a clinician confirms when backup protection can stop. Reversal cannot be guaranteed.

sections.title: Decision guide: compare your priorities
sections.summary: Compare specific measurable priorities and trade-offs, not an algorithm that chooses a method for you.
sections.keywords: best top ranking decision matrix safest least hormone lowest hormones compare choice risk pain insertion fertility
paragraphs: When no added contraceptive hormones and low typical-use pregnancy risk are the priorities, the copper IUD is a useful comparator. External condoms and other barriers avoid placement but have higher fixed typical-use estimates; fertility-awareness methods span a wide range. The chart separates these facts from medical eligibility.
If lower systemic hormone exposure matters

The studied LNG IUDs yielded lower circulating LNG than the specific oral and subdermal products in the pharmacokinetic model. This is not a clinical safety score or a cross-progestin dose comparison.

Pills, patches, rings and barriers avoid a clinician placement procedure. Arm implants involve skin insertion and removal with local anesthesia; both types of IUD require uterine placement. Injections do not require device removal but cannot be undone once given. Pain comparisons between these procedures are not directly established.

Barrier methods have no pharmacologic delay; reversible methods have different average short-term delays. DMPA warrants separate discussion because of prolonged drug action. Avoid treating observational cycles as a waiting instruction.

sections.title: IUD placement, removal & procedure pain
sections.summary: Actual study pain measurements, patient choice and pain-control options.
sections.keywords: pain scale painful insertion removal iud implant numbing anesthesia lidocaine cramping procedure pain score
paragraphs: Pain varies considerably, including for people who have never given birth. Two randomized trials measured insertion pain on a 100-mm visual analog scale. These group medians are not predictions of a particular person's pain or a valid copper-versus-hormonal ranking.

Recent CDC, ACOG and WHO guidance supports discussing local anesthetic approaches. Routine cervical priming with misoprostol has not consistently improved pain and is not routinely advised. A provider should discuss pain control, alternatives and the option to pause or stop; no self-directed medication regimen.

Short-term cramping and spotting may occur. Both IUD types carry risks of expulsion and rare perforation; timing and breastfeeding affect risk. Severe or increasing pain, fever, heavy bleeding or suspected pregnancy with an IUD warrant prompt clinical assessment; severe symptoms may require emergency care.

sections.title: Mental health, mood & emotional wellbeing
sections.summary: Randomized trials and registry observations can tell different stories. Compare their endpoints before interpreting risk.
sections.keywords: mental health depression anxiety mood emotional effects suicide irritability hormonal contraception brain mental side effects
paragraphs: Trial synthesis did not show an average worsening of depressive symptoms among studied adults. A large Danish registry study reported associations with depression-related diagnoses/prescriptions, especially in adolescents. Trial enrollment can exclude vulnerable first-time users; registry designs are affected by confounding and healthcare seeking.

The ECHO ancillary study compared DMPA, copper IUD and an LNG implant over a year; the DMPA group had fewer moderate/severe depressive symptoms than the copper group. No baseline symptom scores were collected, and local preference, switching and missing outcomes matter. Not transferable to every implant or pill.

There is no defensible universal ordering for depression, anxiety, libido or mood. Symptoms can arise with or without contraceptive hormones, and the effect of bleeding, pain and pregnancy anxiety may matter. Discuss new or worsening symptoms with a clinician; seek immediate help for thoughts of self-harm.

sections.title: Libido, sexual comfort & relationship effects
sections.summary: Separate desire, arousal, lubrication, orgasm, discomfort and satisfaction.
sections.keywords: libido sex drive sexual function dryness lubrication intercourse pain desire relationship orgasm
paragraphs: A review of copper and LNG IUD research found generally neutral or favorable desire results, with some evidence of improved sexual pain for LNG IUDs. Other aspects often showed little change. Many studies were observational and heterogeneous.

A 2026 retrospective 90-person cohort observed lower sexual-function scores in LNG IUS users than copper or implant users. Its small self-selected groups cannot distinguish method effects from baseline differences. The ECHO randomized ancillary analysis found no statistically significant sexual dysfunction differences among its three methods at one year.
Do not rank libido from dose

Hormone levels alone cannot determine sexual wellbeing. Bleeding, pelvic discomfort, body image, medications, stress and relationship factors may contribute. Separate method-specific claims from personal experiences and unknowns.

sections.title: Long-term physical health: clots, heart, bones & cancer
sections.summary: Absolute risks, exposure durations and limitations of each study.
sections.keywords: long term effects physical health cancer blood clots stroke heart attack bone density fracture meningioma tumor risks years
paragraphs: A Danish registry cohort compared VTE rates for specific method classes. Absolute rates were low but differed. Confidence intervals and method formulation matter; estimates are associations, not individualized predictions. Eligibility can be more important than an average rate.

A related Danish cohort found associations with some arterial outcomes for both combined and some progestin-only methods. These outcomes cannot be added to the VTE rate or treated as independent replication of it.

UK and Swedish observational research associates hormonal contraceptive use with modestly higher breast cancer risk on average; results vary across exposure timing and formulation. Oral contraceptive evidence also includes lower ovarian/endometrial cancer associations. A 2023 analysis estimated age-dependent 15-year excess breast cancer risk after five years of oral contraceptive use; it is not an annual IUD risk.

A French case-control study found an association between prolonged injectable medroxyprogesterone use and surgery for meningioma. A 2026 Danish study of incident meningioma also found signals for some additional progestogens and high-dose LNG IUD. These are rare outcomes; differing definitions, indications and surveillance can explain differences. Do not infer product-specific safety from absence of a significant signal.

DMPA warrants specific attention to bone density, recovery after stopping and fracture uncertainty. Some progestin-only weight studies identify larger gains with DMPA, while combined-method trial evidence does not establish a large average causal weight effect. Avoid applying injection findings to all hormonal methods.

sections.title: After stopping: miscarriage, birth defects & a future baby
sections.summary: What studies actually measure after contraception ends.
sections.keywords: fertility conceive baby miscarriage birth defects pregnancy outcomes after pill birth control washout infertility
paragraphs: Temporary differences in fecundability should not be confused with permanent infertility. The prospective cohort and multinational survey both suggest longer delays for injections; other reversible methods have shorter estimates.

In PRESTO, prior use of oral contraceptives, IUDs, rings and implants showed little association with miscarriage. Results for patch/injection were uncertain. This study shares population history with CT-07 and is not an independent fertility replication.

A Danish registry study of live births did not find increased major defects with oral contraceptive exposure near pregnancy onset. It cannot establish absence of rare specific effects, apply to all contraceptive routes, or justify using a contraceptive during pregnancy.

Discuss any concerns, removal appointments, health history and preconception care before stopping. A universal detox interval is not supported by these data. Fertility may return before a period; maintain protection until pregnancy is desired.

methods.name: Copper IUD
methods.placement: Clinician uterine placement and removal; variable pain
methods.physical: Heavier bleeding/cramps; device harms; total copper evidence uncertain
methods.mental: No added hormones; mood and sexual effects still variable
methods.fertility: About 2 cycles to usual fecundability in one cohort; may conceive immediately
methods.pro: Long-acting without daily remembering; low pregnancy failure estimate.
methods.con: Heavier periods and cramps; clinician placement/removal; no STI protection.
methods.priceContext: Initial IUD visit example; ask about insertion, anesthesia, follow-up and removal charges.
methods.pain: IUD placement can be painful. Individual pain varies; the trials compared anesthetic approaches, not IUD types.

methods.name: LNG IUD
methods.placement: Clinician uterine placement/removal; pain not reliably ranked by device
methods.physical: Spotting then often lighter bleeding; rare device harms; observational breast/meningioma signals
methods.mental: Systemic exposure is lower in studied LNG comparison; no reliable mood rank
methods.fertility: About 2 cycles in one cohort; pregnancy possible after removal
methods.pro: Low typical-use pregnancy rate; often lighter periods.
methods.con: Progestin reaches blood; spotting, device procedure and uncertain rare long-term associations.
methods.priceContext: Initial IUD visit example; verify device, pain-control and removal coverage.
methods.pain: Same general uterine placement procedure as copper IUD; no reliable pain ranking between devices.

methods.name: Arm implant
methods.placement: Clinician skin insertion and removal with local anesthesia
methods.physical: Irregular bleeding; systemic progestin; vascular/breast evidence formulation-specific
methods.mental: No reliable mood or libido ranking; LNG trial not transferable to all implants
methods.fertility: About 2 cycles in one cohort; pregnancy may occur soon after removal
methods.pro: Long-acting, low typical-use pregnancy rate; reversible by removal.
methods.con: Irregular bleeding; systemic progestin; procedure to remove it.
methods.priceContext: Initial implant example; confirm placement and later removal charges.
methods.pain: Skin insertion and removal with local anesthesia; no comparable numeric pain estimate for ranking against IUD placement.

methods.name: Injection
methods.tradeoff: Repeat injection; possible longer fertility delay
methods.placement: Injection, no removable device; cannot reverse dose
methods.physical: DMPA bone density loss, weight signal, VTE and meningioma associations
methods.mental: Randomized ancillary study did not support worse mood than copper; individual response varies
methods.fertility: Longest temporary delay (about 5–8 cycles) in cohort
methods.pro: No daily pill or implanted device.

evidencePanels.title: Estimated temporary delay in return of usual fecundability
evidencePanels.note: Yland et al. (2020), 17,954 pregnancy planners. Relative to barrier users; approximate modeled time until usual per-cycle conception probability returned, not median time to pregnancy, time to ovulation, or a required wait. Observational, especially uncertain for less common methods.

evidencePanels.title: IUD insertion pain: 2018 randomized trial
evidencePanels.note: 64 nulliparous participants, no-block comparator. p=.002 for insertion pain; block administration itself may cause pain. Not a device comparison or personal pain forecast.

evidencePanels.title: IUD insertion pain: 2026 randomized trial subgroup
evidencePanels.note: Nulliparous subgroup: three arms, overall p<.001. IQRs shown in labels (middle half of observations, not confidence intervals). Do not combine these groups with the 2018 study or compare brands.

evidencePanels.title: Moderate/severe depressive symptoms at 12 months
evidencePanels.note: ECHO ancillary study, South Africa. Group symptom-score threshold, not incident clinical depression. No baseline scores; comparison of copper and injection p=.032; other pairwise comparisons not significant. No general mood ranking.

evidencePanels.title: Venous thromboembolism in Danish registry data (2025)
evidencePanels.note: Yonis et al.; observed standardized rates (95% confidence intervals), not causal risks. Nonuse of hormonal contraception is reference, not specifically copper IUD. Wide intervals for patch/injection; no direct safety ranking. Venous events only.

evidencePanels.title: Estimated excess breast cancers after five years of oral contraception
evidencePanels.unit: Additional cases per 100,000 users over 15 years
evidencePanels.note: Fitzpatrick et al. (2023), modeled absolute excess in high-income countries, during 5 years' use plus 10 after stopping. Two age examples; not annual incidence or applicable to every IUD or progestin.
